West Coast Diamonds

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It's a world that very few have access to... Artisanal Diamond Mining on the West Coast

Unique Selling Point:
The Namaqualand Coastline has lured many adventurers for over a century -- people with a pioneering spirit who leave their comfort zones in search of that one-in-a-million jackpot. Some scour the Atlantic seabed for diamonds, whilst others tunnel into the sand. They share a collective dream of striking it rich, and living an adventure. We meet diamond divers, concessionaires and even illicit artisanal miners, who all have a unique story to tell.


Summary:
The story of privateers, like Engelbrecht, who do manage to get mining concessions is seldom told.
It’s the kind of industry where you either make it big or fail spectacularly. It’s hard work, especially if you’re a diver from shore. These divers spend up to 8 hours a day in the water, often with a family worried about their safety.
They are paid a basic salary and a percentage of the value of diamonds they find. They might go for months earning only their basic salary; some never earn more than that. Not every concessionaire finds diamonds.

Engelbrecht’s other axe to grind is the plight of the people who live on the West Coast, but have never benefited from the abundance of diamonds in the area. The big companies mine when the price is good. When the price drops, they shut the mines and thousands lose their jobs. They keep the concession though and that makes it impossible for privateers, with lower overheads, to mine the area.
The West Coast is one of the poorest areas in South Africa despite being one of the most diamond rich areas in the world.
As part of our story, we want to give these miners a voice. It’s common knowledge that they revert to smuggling to make ends meet. “In die wereld het almal maar ‘n klippies in hulle bosak”, is a common phrase here.
This is after all the wild wild west.

Further information:
It is estimated that there are about 1.5 BILLION carats of alluvial diamonds off the West Coast of SA. No wonder fortune seekers head to Wild West -- but this is no easy life.

The first reported alluvial marine diamond found was in 1908, near Luderitz in Namibia, and the first Namaqualand diamond in 1926. This led to the subsequent discovery of rich diamond fields along the west coast of then German South West Africa. The diamonds found along the coast are characterised by a relatively small size, but exceptional quality -- and these deposits can be successfully exploited with robust geological modelling, experience and low cost operations says Lyndon de Meillon, deputy chair of Sadpo (SA Diamond Producers' Organisation)

Of the estimated seven million carats of diamonds mined in South Africa annually, between 2% to 4% comes from alluvial producers, according to the SA Diamond Producers' Organisation. Obtaining the license is a lengthy and costly process and then they are required to beneficiate 15% of their loot and fork out 5% in export tax. So, for many this is not a get-rich-quickly operation. But people like Engelbrecht cling to the hope that they will strike it rich and many have found ways to circumvent the law. Diamonds are easy to cross borders - metal detectors do no pick them up.
Engelbrecht Rich often travels on commercial flights with a pill bottle filled with diamonds in his top shirt pocket. The value, sometimes a whole month's takings, can be up to R5 million.
“It’s a safe way to transport diamonds”, he says. “Unlike gold it does not set off the airport scanners”.

Studies have shown that the formal diamond mining sector has shrunk by over 90% in the past 20 years, and yet the trade in diamonds is still very much controlled by government and the "big guys"

Diamonds MASTER Script
V/O
This is a story about adventurers. Pioneering spirits who have given up their comfort zones in search of that one-in-a-million jackpot….


…But in order for me to tell this story, I need to go on a bit of an adventure myself… 1300kms to the other side of the country….
V/O Journey…
The journey takes us along the N14, through North West to the Northern Cape…. Past familiar towns … all the way to Kleinzee on the West Coast…
LINK
It’s hard to believe that twenty years ago Kleinzee was a bustling little town. It was established in 1942 as a private alluvial diamond mining settlement, and in its heyday about 4,000 people lived here…, but today it’s mainly a sleepy stopover for tourists.
Ian & JP
Mac: What brings you here?

Ian: Peace, quiet, tranquility… stayed in Gauteng for way too long…
JP
Ek het vir die liefde gekom.

Mac: Liefde? ‘n Meisie?

Ja my vrou is van Komaggas.

I came for love.
Love? A girl?
Yes, my wife is from Komaggas.
V/O
Ian Koster and JP de Jager live here in Kleinzee - a small Namaqualand coastal town… known mainly for spectacular springtime flowers….. And diamonds.
Ian
I had a business in Gauteng which I was running from here and when lockdown came, obviously travel bans, you couldn’t go anywhere. So, ja you need some food on the table. And I met up with some guys who own a mine just outside of town and I said to them, look… I’d like to start working… try and find my fortune, if I’m lucky. And the guy said “well, you’re more than welcome…”
V/O
And just like that the security man from Centurion gave up his business to pursue a very different dream…
Ian
Once you’ve done your first concentrate and you wash it and you take the pan and you turn it over and you see that little glittering thing … I get goosebumps just thinking about it. You’re like a five-year-old kid that sees this massive present under the Xmas tree and it’s a little motorbike - you know the ones that… plastic ones. It’s like that and every single time from that day on when you see it, that’s the feeling you get.
LINK
The area between Alexander Bay in the north, all the way down to the Olifantsriver mouth in the south is rich in alluvial diamond deposits that were transported from the Kimberley region to the coast over a period of about 80 million years… and it’s these diamonds that have called many an adventurer to this part of the world…
JP
Ek dink dis maar net natuurlik. Almal hierso is myners - dis die besigheid van die omgewing.

I think it’s only natural. Everyone here are miners. It’s the business of the area.
V/O
JP is a man with a checkered past, but these days he works for one of the remaining big diamond mining companies in the area - in an open pit mine. Ian has a concession agreement with a local mine just outside Kleinzee where he does what is called - bedrock sweeping. He basically digs into the sand until he finds potholes of gravel in the bedrock.
Ian
Mac: Is it hard work, though?

Oh yes.

Mac: Blood, sweat and tears.

Blood Sweat and tears. We work 12-hour days. Sometimes we have heat - especially in the summers - of about 55 degrees.

Mac: What?

Yes, but then there’s a Southwest wind that comes in and it brings a bit of a cool breeze, but the sun is still killing it.

JP: Daar by ons in die gat kry jy niks wind nie. Dis net son.

There by us in the pit you don’t get any wind. It’s only sun.
V/O
The first alluvial diamond in Namaqualand was found in 1925 near Port Nolloth… and within a year thousands of hopeful diggers rushed to the area. But the Government stepped in and restricted the industry. And although the terrestrial mineral rights were mostly monopolized by De Beers and other big mining giants, individual prospectors looked at the ocean with a glint in their eye…
Johan
What is it that you guys do? What doen julle hierso?

Jis, dit wonder ek self… Nee ons probeer om diamante uit die see uit te haal…

What do you do here?
I wonder about that myself.
No, we try to take out diamonds from the sea.
V/O
Johan Coetzee trained as a diver in the navy in the early 70’s.
Johan
Toe was ek eintlik oppad Walvisbaai toe gewees om op die visbote te gaan werk. Ek het geryloop en toe tel ‘n ou my op en toe vertel hy my van die diamant-duikery op die kus Toe het ek maar hier begin te werk destyds.

Then I was actually on my way to Walvis Bay to go work on the fishing boats.
I was hitchhiking and a guy gave me a lift and told me about the diamond diving on the coast. Then I started working here.


V/O
On-and-off, for over 40 years, Johan has been diving for diamonds.
Johan
Johan: Ja, ek is nou alweer 10-11 jaar terug hierso. Dis is ook maar ‘n geval van ons is nie opgelei in enige ander beroep nie. Ons is duikers, jy weet… so …

Joe: Ek dink, Oom Johan, as eers diamante geduik het en jy’t verlief geraak daarop dan kom jy maar altyd terug.


Ja, I’ve already been back here for ten or eleven years.
It’s also a case of, we’re not trained in any other profession. We are divers, you know.
I think, oom Johan, once you’ve dived for diamonds and fallen in love with it, you’ll always come back.


V/O
And it is this dream that also lured Oom Willie van Rooyen and his family to the West Coast almost 50 years ago…
V/O
We’re on our way, deep into the Namaqua National Park. Oom Willie is taking us to the spot where they started their adventure, but the road ahead is a sandy two-track…
UPSOUND MAC
Because it’s a bit of a sandy road we’ve got to let out a bit of pressure otherwise we’ll be slipping and sliding all over the place and I don’t want to get stuck here at night.
V/O
It’s a bumpy ride down to the Spoegrivier Caves – almost feels like you’re in a boat on the choppy sea…. This is the place the young Willie pitched his tent when he first arrived in Namaqualand.
Oom Willie
Toe’t ons ons tent soontoe geskuif, en ons het die klippe en die gate gebruik vir ons kombuis om ons goeters in te sit.

Then we moved our tent over there, and we used the rocks and holes as our kitchen to put our stuff in.
V/O
The use of pumps to suck up the gravel from the ocean floor was introduced around the time Willie arrived here with his father and brother.
Oom Willie
All over the place people were building these diamond pumps, diamond pumps…

Mac: But Oom Willie, at this time you’re a fisherman from Zululand. You know nothing about diamonds. Who’s teaching you all of this?

Willie: No, it’s common sense.

Mac: Kans vat?

Willie: Ja, kans vat en common sense.
V/O
Willie also learned very early on that diving for diamonds is very hard work…
Oom Willie
You start diving seven o’clock in the morning. And you come up, have a cup of tea, eat a few raisins or whatever then you go down hour and a half come up, till about three o’clock in the afternoon. Then you’re fed up. You’re cold and you’re tired and all that. Then you come back home… Tomorrow morning you go again.


V/O
Operating like a giant “vacuum cleaner”, the pump and compressor are either on land or on a boat, while the diver enters the water with a long suction hose… extracting the gravel from the seabed… sometimes 20-30 meters below.
Oom Willie
We didn’t know anything about decompression and the time you have to dive because you’re diving deeper than 10 meters… You just went down and dived till you get cold and then you come up again…


LINK
As you drive through these lonely plains and almost alien landscapes you can see the damage that mining has done to the environment, but when you start speaking to the people and hearing their stories you see that there’s a whole lot more that’s actually changed….
V/O
As the mining companies scaled down and moved out of the area, it gave the opportunity for so-called “artisanal miners” to move in, looking for their share of the riches.
Steyn
Dit het toe vir ons gesê alraait, ons is werkloos, ons het nie werk nie. Ons is myners, so ons gaan nou dig.

This told us, okay, we are unemployed, we don’t have jobs. We are miners, so we are going to dig.
V/O
The Bontekoe Mine just inland from Kleinzee has been occupied by illegal miners for almost a decade… and at the moment Steyn Crew is the man in charge here…
Steyn
Hulle noem dit Zama-Zama in die black language…

Mac: But it’s artisanal mining, right?

Artisanal mining, yes.
V/O
From the air it looks like a giant termite nest… miners are digging tunnels into the earth…. They run the risk of tunnel cave-ins – which happen all too regularly –, and endure harsh working conditions … all in the name of making money….
Steyn
Hier sal jy sien, hier is nou van die gruis wat die ouens gebring het. Hulle het die gruis gebring so hulle sakke is nou gereed om deur die jig gesit te word.

Mac: But now how do you know… wie se gruis is wie sin?

Alraait, u sal sien soos daai dame daarso. Sy sit by haar gruis. Elke een het sy hopie.

Mac: waar kry hulle die hopies?

Oral waar hulle myn.

Here you will see some of the gravel the guys brought here. They brought the gravel so their bags are ready to be put through the jig.

Whose gravel is whose?

Okay, you see that lady over there? She sits with her gravel. Everyone has his pile, so the gravel doesn’t get mixed up.

Where do you get the gravel?
Everywhere they’re mining.
V/O
In the jig, the gravel is washed and separated… The waste is expelled and the potential diamond containing concentrate is caught in a series of sieves.
Steyn
As dit klaar gewas is dan word die siwwe uitgehaal – ons noem dit die tafel - dan word hulle op die tafel gesit. En dan word hulle geblaai en dan kyk hulle vir die diamante.

Mac: Nou hoe blaai hulle?

Hulle gebruik sommer ‘n mes.

Once it’s been washed the sieves are taken out. We call it the table, then it is put on the table. Then it gets combed and then they look for the diamonds.
Now, how do they comb?
They use a knife.


Mac: Hoekom gebruik julle ‘n mes?

Dis maar een van onse tools.

Mac: Okay

Ja hy lig hom baie maklik so met die lem uit. Want as hy hom so met die vinger vat dan druk jy die ander diamante af.

Mac: Ja

En omdat die mes mos maar ‘n deel is van jou tools wat jy saam met jou…

Mac: Maar die mes lyk nie vir diamante nie…

Dit is ‘n biltong-mes

Why do you use a knife?
It is one of our tools.
Ja, it lifts the diamond easily with the blade, because if you use your fingers you push the other diamonds down.
So, that’s why the knife is much better and a knife is one of the tools you carry with you.
But this knife doesn’t look like it’s for diamonds.
It’s a biltong knife.
V/o
And sometimes… the effort pays off!
Miner
Harde werk vir hom… en hy’s so klein…

Hard work for it
And it’s so small.
Ian
Mac: Would you do anything else?

Right now? No, I still have to find the one with my name on it.

Mac: that 20 carater?

No. it’s a 40.02 - I’ve dreamt of it 4 times. I just don’t know where it is!
Oom Willie
You’ve got two, two choices… Or you come and work diamonds, or you play horses. It’s the same thing. You’re going to lose money anyway.
V/O
And perhaps that realisation is worth more than the precious stones concealed in this unforgiving place; knowing that while not everyone who dreams big, makes it big, there’s value to be found in the search.






***
PROMO 1 11”
LINK: From tunneling into the ground to vacuuming the ocean floor. For over a century fortune seekers have been trying their luck and hoping to strike it rich.


PROMO 2 21”
Diamonds have lured many an adventurer to the Namaqualand coast for almost a century, but not everyone who dreams big… makes it big!

UPSOUND: Or you come and work diamonds, or you play horses. It’s the same thing.
PROMO 3 21”
The West Coast is all about diamonds and for almost a century artisanal miners have flocked to the area with a glint in their eye.

UPSOUND: Ons almal hoop maar eendag vir daai jackpot, of iets wat jou gaan help.

UPSOUND: Do you ever find diamonds here? Always. Always? Elke dag? No I will not say every day, than the rest of the world will see and they’ll come.

Dis is ook maar ‘n geval van ons is nie opgelei in enige ander beroep nie. Ons is duikers, jy weet… so … Joe: Ek dink, Oom Johan, as eers diamante geduik het en jy’t verlief geraak daarop dan kom jy maar altyd terug. Ja, I’ve already been back here for ten or eleven years. It’s also a case of, we’re not trained in any other profession. We are divers, you know. I think, oom Johan, once you’ve dived for diamonds and fallen in love with it, you’ll always come back. V/O And it is this dream that also lured Oom Willie van Rooyen and his family to the West Coast almost 50 years ago… V/O We’re on our way, deep into the Namaqua National Park. Oom Willie is taking us to the spot where they started their adventure, but the road ahead is a sandy two-track… UPSOUND MAC Because it’s a bit of a sandy road we’ve got to let out a bit of pressure otherwise we’ll be slipping and sliding all over the place and I don’t want to get stuck here at night. V/O It’s a bumpy ride down to the Spoegrivier Caves – almost feels like you’re in a boat on the choppy sea…. This is the place the young Willie pitched his tent when he first arrived in Namaqualand. Oom Willie Toe’t ons ons tent soontoe geskuif, en ons het die klippe en die gate gebruik vir ons kombuis om ons goeters in te sit. Then we moved our tent over there, and we used the rocks and holes as our kitchen to put our stuff in. V/O The use of pumps to suck up the gravel from the ocean floor was introduced around the time Willie arrived here with his father and brother. Oom Willie All over the place people were building these diamond pumps, diamond pumps… Mac: But Oom Willie, at this time you’re a fisherman from Zululand. You know nothing about diamonds. Who’s teaching you all of this? Willie: No, it’s common sense. Mac: Kans vat? Willie: Ja, kans vat en common sense. V/O Willie also learned very early on that diving for diamonds is very hard work… Oom Willie You start diving seven o’clock in the morning. And you come up, have a cup of tea, eat a few raisins or whatever then you go down hour and a half come up, till about three o’clock in the afternoon. Then you’re fed up. You’re cold and you’re tired and all that. Then you come back home… Tomorrow morning you go again. V/O Operating like a giant “vacuum cleaner”, the pump and compressor are either on land or on a boat, while the diver enters the water with a long suction hose… extracting the gravel from the seabed… sometimes 20-30 meters below. Oom Willie We didn’t know anything about decompression and the time you have to dive because you’re diving deeper than 10 meters… You just went down and dived till you get cold and then you come up again… LINK As you drive through these lonely plains and almost alien landscapes you can see the damage that mining has done to the environment, but when you start speaking to the people and hearing their stories you see that there’s a whole lot more that’s actually changed…. V/O As the mining companies scaled down and moved out of the area, it gave the opportunity for so-called “artisanal miners” to move in, looking for their share of the riches. Steyn Dit het toe vir ons gesê alraait, ons is werkloos, ons het nie werk nie. Ons is myners, so ons gaan nou dig. This told us, okay, we are unemployed, we don’t have jobs. We are miners, so we are going to dig. V/O The Bontekoe Mine just inland from Kleinzee has been occupied by illegal miners for almost a decade… and at the moment Steyn Crew is the man in charge here… Steyn Hulle noem dit Zama-Zama in die black language… Mac: But it’s artisanal mining, right? Artisanal mining, yes. V/O From the air it looks like a giant termite nest… miners are digging tunnels into the earth…. They run the risk of tunnel cave-ins – which happen all too regularly –, and endure harsh working conditions … all in the name of making money…. Steyn Hier sal jy sien, hier is nou van die gruis wat die ouens gebring het. Hulle het die gruis gebring so hulle sakke is nou gereed om deur die jig gesit te word. Mac: But now how do you know… wie se gruis is wie sin? Alraait, u sal sien soos daai dame daarso. Sy sit by haar gruis. Elke een het sy hopie. Mac: waar kry hulle die hopies? Oral waar hulle myn. Here you will see some of the gravel the guys brought here. They brought the gravel so their bags are ready to be put through the jig. Whose gravel is whose? Okay, you see that lady over there? She sits with her gravel. Everyone has his pile, so the gravel doesn’t get mixed up. Where do you get the gravel? Everywhere they’re mining. V/O In the jig, the gravel is washed and separated… The waste is expelled and the potential diamond containing concentrate is caught in a series of sieves. Steyn As dit klaar gewas is dan word die siwwe uitgehaal – ons noem dit die tafel - dan word hulle op die tafel gesit. En dan word hulle geblaai en dan kyk hulle vir die diamante. Mac: Nou hoe blaai hulle? Hulle gebruik sommer ‘n mes. Once it’s been washed the sieves are taken out. We call it the table, then it is put on the table. Then it gets combed and then they look for the diamonds. Now, how do they comb? They use a knife. Mac: Hoekom gebruik julle ‘n mes? Dis maar een van onse tools. Mac: Okay Ja hy lig hom baie maklik so met die lem uit. Want as hy hom so met die vinger vat dan druk jy die ander diamante af. Mac: Ja En omdat die mes mos maar ‘n deel is van jou tools wat jy saam met jou… Mac: Maar die mes lyk nie vir diamante nie… Dit is ‘n biltong-mes Why do you use a knife? It is one of our tools. Ja, it lifts the diamond easily with the blade, because if you use your fingers you push the other diamonds down. So, that’s why the knife is much better and a knife is one of the tools you carry with you. But this knife doesn’t look like it’s for diamonds. It’s a biltong knife. V/o And sometimes… the effort pays off! Miner Harde werk vir hom… en hy’s so klein… Hard work for it And it’s so small. Ian Mac: Would you do anything else? Right now? No, I still have to find the one with my name on it. Mac: that 20 carater? No. it’s a 40.02 - I’ve dreamt of it 4 times. I just don’t know where it is! Oom Willie You’ve got two, two choices… Or you come and work diamonds, or you play horses. It’s the same thing. You’re going to lose money anyway. V/O And perhaps that realisation is worth more than the precious stones concealed in this unforgiving place; knowing that while not everyone who dreams big, makes it big, there’s value to be found in the search. *** PROMO 1 11” LINK: From tunneling into the ground to vacuuming the ocean floor. For over a century fortune seekers have been trying their luck and hoping to strike it rich. PROMO 2 21” Diamonds have lured many an adventurer to the Namaqualand coast for almost a century, but not everyone who dreams big… makes it big! UPSOUND: Or you come and work diamonds, or you play horses. It’s the same thing. PROMO 3 21” The West Coast is all about diamonds and for almost a century artisanal miners have flocked to the area with a glint in their eye. UPSOUND: Ons almal hoop maar eendag vir daai jackpot, of iets wat jou gaan help. UPSOUND: Do you ever find diamonds here? Always. Always? Elke dag? No I will not say every day, than the rest of the world will see and they’ll come.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It's a world that very few have access to... Artisanal Diamond Mining on the West Coast
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Namaqualand Coastline has lured many adventurers for over a century -- people with a pioneering spirit who leave their comfort zones in search of that one-in-a-million jackpot. Some scour the Atlantic seabed for diamonds, whilst others tunnel into the sand. They share a collective dream of striking it rich, and living an adventure. We meet diamond divers, concessionaires and even illicit artisanal miners, who all have a unique story to tell.
metadata.Summary: The story of privateers, like Engelbrecht, who do manage to get mining concessions is seldom told. It’s the kind of industry where you either make it big or fail spectacularly. It’s hard work, especially if you’re a diver from shore. These divers spend up to 8 hours a day in the water, often with a family worried about their safety. They are paid a basic salary and a percentage of the value of diamonds they find. They might go for months earning only their basic salary; some never earn more than that. Not every concessionaire finds diamonds. Engelbrecht’s other axe to grind is the plight of the people who live on the West Coast, but have never benefited from the abundance of diamonds in the area. The big companies mine when the price is good. When the price drops, they shut the mines and thousands lose their jobs. They keep the concession though and that makes it impossible for privateers, with lower overheads, to mine the area. The West Coast is one of the poorest areas in South Africa despite being one of the most diamond rich areas in the world. As part of our story, we want to give these miners a voice. It’s common knowledge that they revert to smuggling to make ends meet. “In die wereld het almal maar ‘n klippies in hulle bosak”, is a common phrase here. This is after all the wild wild west.
metadata.Further information: It is estimated that there are about 1.5 BILLION carats of alluvial diamonds off the West Coast of SA. No wonder fortune seekers head to Wild West -- but this is no easy life. The first reported alluvial marine diamond found was in 1908, near Luderitz in Namibia, and the first Namaqualand diamond in 1926. This led to the subsequent discovery of rich diamond fields along the west coast of then German South West Africa. The diamonds found along the coast are characterised by a relatively small size, but exceptional quality -- and these deposits can be successfully exploited with robust geological modelling, experience and low cost operations says Lyndon de Meillon, deputy chair of Sadpo (SA Diamond Producers' Organisation) Of the estimated seven million carats of diamonds mined in South Africa annually, between 2% to 4% comes from alluvial producers, according to the SA Diamond Producers' Organisation. Obtaining the license is a lengthy and costly process and then they are required to beneficiate 15% of their loot and fork out 5% in export tax. So, for many this is not a get-rich-quickly operation. But people like Engelbrecht cling to the hope that they will strike it rich and many have found ways to circumvent the law. Diamonds are easy to cross borders - metal detectors do no pick them up. Engelbrecht Rich often travels on commercial flights with a pill bottle filled with diamonds in his top shirt pocket. The value, sometimes a whole month's takings, can be up to R5 million. “It’s a safe way to transport diamonds”, he says. “Unlike gold it does not set off the airport scanners”. Studies have shown that the formal diamond mining sector has shrunk by over 90% in the past 20 years, and yet the trade in diamonds is still very much controlled by government and the "big guys"
